title: The Weaver Who Invented Global Cotton Standardization
event_summary: In 1790, a master Bengali weaver named Taher Ali, working in the muslin workshops of Dhaka, developed a precise thread-count grading system for muslin cloth that classified fabrics from coarse to the legendary 'abrawan' (running water) grade. His system used standardized reed widths and warp-thread densities to guarantee consistent quality across hundreds of independent weavers supplying the East India Company. This grading framework was so effective that British textile merchants adopted and adapted it as the basis for thread-count classification in Manchester mills, creating the global standard by which cotton fabric quality is still measured today.
why_forgotten: The British East India Company systematically destroyed Bengal's muslin industry through punitive tariffs and forced de-industrialization, making it politically inconvenient to credit Bengali artisans with foundational textile science. Colonial narratives attributed cotton standardization to British factory innovation, erasing indigenous technical knowledge. Taher Ali's name survived only in fragmentary Company records and a single Persian-language trade ledger rediscovered in the 1970s by Bangladeshi historian Abdul Karim.
why_it_matters: Every modern textile label citing thread count—from Egyptian cotton sheets to surgical gauze specifications—traces its measurement logic back to Bengali weaving standards. The destruction of Dhaka's muslin industry is now recognized as one of the first cases of deliberate colonial de-industrialization, a template repeated across colonized economies. Bangladesh's modern dominance in garment manufacturing represents an ironic return to its historical role as the world's most sophisticated textile production center.
